name: Hebes Mensa deposit
geo: Hebes Chasma is an enclosed trough in the Valles Marineris system with no outlet. Hebes Mensa, the massive interior layered deposit, rises ~8 km from the chasma floor. Sulfate and phyllosilicate-bearing ILDs record prolonged aqueous diagenesis and are among the thickest sedimentary sequences on Mars.
cite: Schmidt, G., Fueten, F., Stesky, R., Flahaut, J., & Hauber, E. (2018). Geology of Hebes Chasma, Mars: 1. Structure, stratigraphy, and mineralogy of the interior layered deposits. Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets, 123(11), 2893–2919. https://doi.org/10.1029/2018JE005658
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: Landon Valles basin
geo: Landon Valles is a Noachian valley network system recording peak fluvial activity ~3.7 Ga. Basin-filling lacustrine sediments in the terminal basin potentially preserve a habitability record from early Mars. The global valley network mapping by Hynek et al. classifies this as a second-order tributary system.
cite: Hynek, B. M., Beach, M., & Hoke, M. R. T. (2010). Updated global map of Martian valley networks and implications for climate and hydrologic processes. Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets, 115(E9), Article E09008. https://doi.org/10.1029/2009JE003548
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: Noachis Terra Craters
geo: Noachis Terra is among the oldest preserved terrains on Mars (~4.0 Ga), densely cratered and dissected by Noachian valley networks. Impact craters preserve phyllosilicate-bearing ejecta blankets, and the valley network density records peak fluvial activity during the late Noachian–early Hesperian transition.
cite: Fassett, C. I., & Head, J. W. (2008). Valley network-fed, open-basin lakes on Mars: Distribution and implications for Noachian surface and subsurface hydrology. Icarus, 198(1), 37–56. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.icarus.2008.06.016
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: Arcadia Planitia
geo: Arcadia Planitia in the northern lowlands hosts some of the highest near-surface ice content inferred on Mars from neutron spectrometry. Scalloped depressions, polygon networks, and layered ejecta craters record active periglacial processes driven by Amazonian ground ice.
cite: Kadish, S., Head, J., Parsons, R., & Marchant, D. (2008). The Ascraeus Mons fan-shaped deposit: Volcano-ice interactions and the climatic implications of cold-based tropical mountain glaciation. Icarus, 197(1), 84–109. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.icarus.2008.03.019
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: Chaos Terrain
geo: Martian chaotic terrain forms through catastrophic subsidence following drainage of subsurface volatiles, ice or pressurized groundwater. The resulting knobby remnant mesas and intervening depressions are genetically linked to outflow channel initiation and some of the largest known flood events in the Solar System.
cite: Rodriguez, J., Sasaki, S., Kuzmin, R., Dohm, J., Tanaka, K., Miyamoto, H., Kurita, K., Komatsu, G., Fairen, A., & Ferris, J. (2005). Outflow channel sources, reactivation, and chaos formation, Xanthe Terra, Mars. Icarus, 175(1), 36–57. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.icarus.2004.10.025
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: Gullies Tempe Terra
geo: Tempe Terra hosts one of the densest concentrations of Martian gullies, alcove-channel-apron systems incised into crater walls and hillslopes. Their geologically recent formation age and morphology suggest seasonal CO₂ frost-driven debris flows as the dominant formation mechanism.
cite: Pilorget, C., & Forget, F. (2016). Formation of gullies on Mars by debris flows triggered by CO₂ sublimation. Nature Geoscience, 9(1), 65–69. https://doi.org/10.1038/ngeo2619
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: Gorgonum Chaos
geo: Gorgonum Chaos in Terra Sirenum is a chaotic depression associated with concentrated chloride and sulfate salt deposits, among the largest chloride exposures on Mars. One of the densest gully fields on Mars is also found here, interpreted as evidence of recent episodic liquid water activity.
cite: Osterloo, M. M., Hamilton, V. E., Bandfield, J. L., Glotch, T. D., Baldridge, A. M., Christensen, P. R., Tornabene, L. L., & Anderson, F. S. (2008). Chloride-bearing materials in the southern highlands of Mars. Science, 319(5870), 1651–1654. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1150690
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: Uranius Mons Crater
geo: Uranius Mons is a low-relief paterae-type shield volcano in the Tharsis region. Impact craters on its flanks record multiple Amazonian resurfacing episodes. Its summit caldera and radial graben system indicate a complex magmatic history distinct from the large Tharsis Montes.
cite: Hauber, E., Bleacher, J., Gwinner, K., Williams, D., & Greeley, R. (2009). The topography and morphology of low shields and associated landforms of plains volcanism in the Tharsis region of Mars. Journal of Volcanology and Geothermal Research, 185(1-2), 69–95. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jvolgeores.2009.04.015
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: Aeolis Planum
geo: Aeolis Planum flanks Gale Crater and hosts an extensive yardang field, wind-sculpted ridges formed by differential erosion of indurated sedimentary layers. The region records late Hesperian to Amazonian aeolian reworking of lacustrine deposits adjacent to the MSL Curiosity rover field site.
cite: Zimbelman, J. R., & Scheidt, S. P. (2012). Hesperian age for western Medusae Fossae Formation, Mars. Science, 336(6089), 1683. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1221094
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: Phlegra Montes Valley
geo: Phlegra Montes is a NW-trending mountain range bordering the northern lowlands, with valley systems exhibiting lobate debris aprons, the surface expression of debris-covered glaciers. These represent the most direct evidence for extant non-polar ground ice on Mars.
cite: Levy, J. S., Fassett, C. I., Head, J. W., Schwartz, C., & Watters, J. L. (2014). Sequestered glacial ice contribution to the global Martian water budget: Geometric constraints on the volume of remnant, midlatitude debris-covered glaciers. Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets, 119(10), 2188–2196. https://doi.org/10.1002/2014JE004685
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: Pasteur Crater
geo: Pasteur Crater in Arabia Terra contains finely-laminated interior layered deposits (ILDs) interpreted as aeolian or lacustrine sedimentary sequences. Arabia Terra hosts one of Mars' largest concentrations of layered sedimentary basins, potentially recording Hesperian hydrological activity.
cite: Edgett, K. S., & Malin, M. C. (2002). Martian sedimentary rock stratigraphy: Outcrops and interbedded craters of northwest Sinus Meridiani and southwest Arabia Terra. Geophysical Research Letters, 29(24), 2179. https://doi.org/10.1029/2002GL016515
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: Olympus Mons Systems
geo: Olympus Mons is the largest shield volcano in the Solar System, rising ~22 km above the surrounding plains with a basal escarpment exceeding 8 km. Lava flow systems on the flanks preserve primary Amazonian volcanic stratigraphy; the summit caldera records multiple collapse episodes from complex magmatic evolution.
cite: Mouginis-Mark, P. J., & Rowland, S. K. (2001). The geomorphology of planetary calderas. Geomorphology, 37(3-4), 201–223. https://doi.org/10.1016/s0169-555x(00)00083-0
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: Argyre Planitia Valley
geo: Argyre Planitia is a 1,800 km impact basin reaching −5.2 km, the deepest on Mars. Valley networks on its rim record late Noachian fluvial incision, and glacial flow indicators including lobate debris aprons suggest Late Amazonian ice sheet occupation of the basin interior.
cite: Hiesinger, H., & Head, J. W., III (2002). Topography and morphology of the Argyre Basin, Mars: Implications for its geologic and hydrologic history. Planetary and Space Science, 50(10-11), 939–981. https://doi.org/10.1016/s0032-0633(02)00054-5
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: Oxia Colles
geo: Oxia Colles forms the knobby highland remnant terrain on the western margin of the clay-bearing Oxia Planum plain. These erosional remnants of Noachian crust at the crustal dichotomy boundary expose Fe/Mg smectite-bearing bedrock detected by CRISM and OMEGA spectrometers.
cite: Carter, J., Poulet, F., Bibring, J., Mangold, N., & Murchie, S. (2013). Hydrous minerals on Mars as seen by the CRISM and OMEGA imaging spectrometers: Updated global view. Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets, 118(4), 831–858. https://doi.org/10.1029/2012JE004145
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: Coogoon Valles
geo: Coogoon Valles is a sinuous valley system draining into Oxia Planum, the ExoMars Rosalind Franklin landing site. Its delta fan at the basin outlet preserves Noachian fluvial and lacustrine sediments rich in Fe/Mg phyllosilicates, making it a key astrobiological target.
cite: Quantin-Nataf, C., Carter, J., Mandon, L., Thollot, P., Balme, M., Volat, M., Pan, L., Loizeau, D., Millot, C., Breton, S., Dehouck, E., Fawdon, P., Gupta, S., Davis, J., Grindrod, P. M., Pacifici, A., Bultel, B., Allemand, P., Ody, A., … Broyer, J. (2021). Oxia Planum: The landing site for the ExoMars Rosalind Franklin rover mission. Astrobiology, 21(3), 345–366. https://doi.org/10.1089/ast.2019.2191
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: Aram Chaos
geo: Aram Chaos is a ~280 km crater that collapsed catastrophically following destabilization of a subsurface cryosphere. TES grey hematite detections indicate past aqueous mineralization. The chaotic knobby interior records some of Mars' most violent water-release events.
cite: Glotch, T. D., & Christensen, P. R. (2005). Geologic and mineralogic mapping of Aram Chaos: Evidence for a water-rich history. Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets, 110(E9), Article E09006. https://doi.org/10.1029/2004JE002389
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: South Polar Deposits
geo: Near 89°S the SPLD residual cap hosts active CO₂ slab sublimation features ('swiss-cheese terrain') documenting present-day volatile transport. HiRISE multi-temporal imaging revealed annual changes in these features, providing a direct record of modern Martian climate.
cite: Thomas, P. C., James, P. B., Calvin, W. M., Haberle, R., & Malin, M. C. (2009). Residual south polar cap of Mars: Stratigraphy, history, and implications of recent changes. Icarus, 203(2), 352–375. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.icarus.2009.05.014
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: North Polar Layered Deposits Bench
geo: North Polar Layered Deposit bench scarps expose ~2 km of stratigraphy spanning ~5 Myr of obliquity-paced accumulation. SHARAD detected internal unconformities interpreted as high-obliquity erosional episodes. Individual layers 1–10 m thick serve as a Martian equivalent of ice-core climate proxies.
cite: Putzig, N. E., Phillips, R. J., Campbell, B. A., Holt, J. W., Plaut, J. J., Carter, L. M., Egan, A. F., Bernardini, F., Safaeinili, A., & Seu, R. (2009). Subsurface structure of Planum Boreum from Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter Shallow Radar soundings. Icarus, 204(2), 443–457. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.icarus.2009.07.034
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: South Polar Deposits
geo: The South Polar Layered Deposits (SPLD) are a ~3 km-thick stack of alternating ice-rich and dust-laden layers recording obliquity-driven Martian climate cycles over tens of millions of years. SHARAD radar soundings resolved the internal stratigraphy and confirmed near-pure water ice composition.
cite: Plaut, J. J., Picardi, G., Safaeinili, A., Ivanov, A. B., Milkovich, S. M., Cicchetti, A., Kofman, W., Mouginot, J., Farrell, W. M., Phillips, R. J., Clifford, S. M., Frigeri, A., Orosei, R., Federico, C., Williams, I. P., Gurnett, D. A., Nielsen, E., Hagfors, T., Heggy, E., … Edenhofer, P. (2007). Subsurface radar sounding of the south polar layered deposits of Mars. Science, 316(5821), 92–95. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1139672
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: Cavil Angusti South Polar
geo: Cavi Angusti comprises deep, steep-walled pits cut into the Hesperian Dorsa Argentea Formation beside the south polar layered deposits. The formation is interpreted as the deposit of a former south circumpolar ice sheet that melted and retreated; here the cavi expose ~1.7 km of relief.
cite: Tanaka, K. L., & Kolb, E. J. (2001). Geologic history of the polar regions of Mars based on Mars Global Surveyor data: I. Noachian and Hesperian periods. Icarus, 154(1), 3–21. https://doi.org/10.1006/icar.2001.6675
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: Brain Terrain
geo: Brain terrain is a convoluted ridge-and-cell surface texture, ~3–5 m in relief, formed by the sublimation of buried mid-latitude excess ice. Its closed-cell morphology is a diagnostic marker of subsurface volatile loss and ground-ice degradation in the northern mid-latitudes.
cite: Levy, J., Head, J., & Marchant, D. (2009). Thermal contraction crack polygons on Mars: Classification, distribution, and climate implications from HiRISE observations. Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets, 114(E1), Article E01007. https://doi.org/10.1029/2008JE003273
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: Terra Sirenum
geo: Terra Sirenum is a heavily cratered Noachian highland hosting chloride salt deposits and Fe/Mg phyllosilicates. These mineral assemblages record ancient aqueous environments and episodic surface water, making the region a key archive of early Martian habitability in the southern hemisphere.
cite: Osterloo, M. M., Anderson, F. S., Hamilton, V. E., & Hynek, B. M. (2010). Geologic context of proposed chloride-bearing materials on Mars. Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets, 115(E10), Article E10012. https://doi.org/10.1029/2010JE003613
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: SpaceX Starship Arcadia
geo: Arcadia Planitia is a smooth northern mid-latitude plain underlain in places by a widespread, decameters-thick layer of excess water ice. Terraced impact craters and SHARAD radar reflections indicate that this buried ice is volumetrically significant, making the region important for periglacial stratigraphy, recent climate history, and future landing-site resource assessment.
cite: Bramson, A. M., Byrne, S., Putzig, N. E., Sutton, S., Plaut, J. J., Brothers, T. C., & Holt, J. W. (2015). Widespread excess ice in Arcadia Planitia, Mars. Geophysical Research Letters, 42(16), 6566–6574. https://doi.org/10.1002/2015GL064844
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: Protonilus Mensae Ridges
geo: Protonilus Mensae lies along the northern dichotomy boundary in classic fretted terrain containing lobate debris aprons and lineated valley fill. These flow-related landforms are widely interpreted as remnants of Late Amazonian debris-covered glacial systems, preserving evidence for substantial mid-latitude ice accumulation and subsequent sublimation beneath protective debris.
cite: Head, J. W., Marchant, D. R., Dickson, J. L., Kress, A. M., & Baker, D. M. (2010). Northern mid-latitude glaciation in the Late Amazonian period of Mars: Criteria for the recognition of debris-covered glacier and valley glacier landsystem deposits. Earth and Planetary Science Letters, 294(3-4), 306–320. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.epsl.2009.06.041
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: Phlegra Dorsa Cone Field
geo: Phlegra Dorsa contains abundant small-cone morphologies whose spatial patterns contribute to studies of Martian volcanic, sedimentary, and periglacial processes. High-resolution HiRISE mapping of cone fields provides morphometric constraints on cone geometry and distribution, supporting comparison among competing formation mechanisms across Mars.
cite: Yang, C., Zhang, N., Guan, R., & Zhao, H. (2024). Mapping cones on Mars in high-resolution planetary images with deep learning-based instance segmentation. Remote Sensing, 16(2), Article 227. https://doi.org/10.3390/rs16020227
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: High Latitude Exposure
geo: The north polar layered deposits are a thick sequence of water-ice-rich and dust-bearing strata exposed in troughs near Planum Boreum. HiRISE stereo DTMs resolve the topographic expression of individual layers and permit stratigraphic correlations through hundreds of meters of section, supporting interpretation of the NPLD as a high-resolution archive of recent Martian climate variability.
cite: Becerra, P., Byrne, S., Sori, M. M., Sutton, S., & Herkenhoff, K. E. (2016). Stratigraphy of the north polar layered deposits of Mars from high-resolution topography. Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets, 121(8), 1445–1471. https://doi.org/10.1002/2015JE004992
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: Pits Sinai Planum
geo: Sinai Planum is part of the tectonically fractured plateau surrounding the Valles Marineris–Tharsis region, where pits and troughs commonly occur with extensional structures. Martian pit-crater chains are generally interpreted as collapse features developed above subsurface cavities, and structural associations indicate that dilational normal faults and extension fractures are a major formation mechanism.
cite: Wyrick, D., Ferrill, D. A., Morris, A. P., Colton, S. L., & Sims, D. W. (2004). Distribution, morphology, and origins of Martian pit crater chains. Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets, 109(E6), Article E06005. https://doi.org/10.1029/2004JE002240
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: Mesa Utopia Planitia
geo: Utopia Planitia occupies a giant Noachian impact basin in the northern lowlands whose present morphology reflects extensive sedimentary and volcanic infilling as well as later tectonic modification. Mesas and other remnant relief within the plains preserve local stratigraphic and structural information that helps constrain the basin's long post-impact resurfacing history.
cite: Thomson, B. J., & Head, J. W. (2001). Utopia Basin, Mars: Characterization of topography and morphology and assessment of the origin and evolution of basin internal structure. Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets, 106(E10), 23209–23230. https://doi.org/10.1029/2000JE001355
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: Bernard Crater Channels
geo: Bernard Crater is a large impact basin in the Terra Sirenum highlands. Sinuous channels incised into its floor record surface or near-surface water flow after the crater formed, linking this site to the broader record of valley-network activity that shaped the southern highlands during the Noachian and early Hesperian.
cite: Hynek, B. M., Beach, M., & Hoke, M. R. T. (2010). Updated global map of Martian valley networks and implications for climate and hydrologic processes. Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets, 115(E9), Article E09008. https://doi.org/10.1029/2009JE003548
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: Maja Valles
geo: Maja Valles is a large outflow channel that drains from the Valles Marineris region northward across Lunae Planum into Chryse Planitia. Streamlined islands, scoured floors, and cataracts record catastrophic Hesperian floods released from the subsurface. The README notes extra noise on the west side of this DTM from jitter in the parent stereo pair; consult the FOM map before analysis.
cite: Baker, V. R., & Kochel, R. C. (1979). Martian channel morphology: Maja and Kasei Valles. Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth, 84(B14), 7961–7983. https://doi.org/10.1029/JB084IB14P07961
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: Crater Adjacent Lunae Mensa
geo: This crater sits against the Lunae Mensa scarp at the eastern edge of the Kasei Valles flood system, where catastrophic outflow carved kilometer-scale cliffs into Lunae Planum. With nearly 2.75 km of relief, the DTM captures the scarp, the crater, and the scoured channel floor in a single product.
cite: Robinson, M. S., & Tanaka, K. L. (1990). Magnitude of a catastrophic flood event at Kasei Valles, Mars. Geology, 18(9), 902–905. https://doi.org/10.1130/0091-7613(1990)018<0902:moacfe>2.3.co;2
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: Small Mounds Chryse Planitia
geo: Chryse Planitia hosts fields of small, often cratered mounds at the terminus of the circum-Chryse outflow channels. Their morphology and setting have been compared with terrestrial mud volcanoes, which would point to fluid-rich sediment rising from depth after the floods. This DTM has the lowest total RMS (0.090 px) in the portfolio.
cite: Komatsu, G., Okubo, C. H., Wray, J. J., Ojha, L., Cardinale, M., Murana, A., Orosei, R., Chan, M. A., Ormö, J., & Gallagher, R. (2016). Small edifice features in Chryse Planitia, Mars: Assessment of a mud volcano hypothesis. Icarus, 268, 56–75. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.icarus.2015.12.032
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: Flute Casts Ares Vallis
geo: Ares Vallis is one of the major outflow channels draining into Chryse Planitia near the Mars Pathfinder landing site. Possible flute casts, scour marks formed by turbulent flood water eroding the channel floor, preserve the flow direction and energy of the catastrophic floods that carved the valley.
cite: Komatsu, G., & Baker, V. R. (1997). Paleohydrology and flood geomorphology of Ares Vallis. Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets, 102(E2), 4151–4160. https://doi.org/10.1029/96JE02564
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: Terraced Crater
geo: This terraced crater formed on the ejecta of a larger crater in the northern mid-latitudes. Terraces inside small craters form when an impact excavates a layered target with a strength contrast, such as an ice-rich layer over stronger material, so terrace depths can be used to estimate the thickness of buried excess ice.
cite: Bramson, A. M., Byrne, S., Putzig, N. E., Sutton, S., Plaut, J. J., Brothers, T. C., & Holt, J. W. (2015). Widespread excess ice in Arcadia Planitia, Mars. Geophysical Research Letters, 42(16), 6566–6574. https://doi.org/10.1002/2015GL064844
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: Troughs Ridges Chryse Planitia
geo: At the northern reach of Chryse Planitia, where the circum-Chryse outflow channels open into the northern lowlands, troughs and ridges cut the plains. Trough networks in the northern plains have long been used to test how the thick lowland fill compacted, cooled, and deformed after emplacement, so measured trough widths, depths, and wall slopes from this DTM constrain those models directly.
cite: Pechmann, J. C. (1980). The origin of polygonal troughs on the northern plains of Mars. Icarus, 42(2), 185–210. https://doi.org/10.1016/0019-1035(80)90071-8
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: Dunes Kaltain
geo: The Kaltain dunes lie in the north polar sand sea that rings the residual ice cap. Each winter a seasonal carbon-dioxide frost layer blankets the dunes; as it sublimates in spring, gas flow and frost-driven slumping erode the slip faces, and summer winds restore them, making this field a monitor of present-day sediment transport. The README cautions that the dunes leave significant artifacts at short wavelengths; consult the FOM map before measuring small-scale topography.
cite: Hansen, C. J., Bourke, M., Bridges, N. T., Byrne, S., Colon, C., Diniega, S., Dundas, C., Herkenhoff, K., McEwen, A., Mellon, M., Portyankina, G., & Thomas, N. (2011). Seasonal erosion and restoration of Mars’ northern polar dunes. Science, 331(6017), 575–578. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1197636
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: Dark Linear Ridges Southern
geo: Dark linear ridges cross the southern high-latitude highlands here. Elongate ridges in the circum-south-polar region are commonly interpreted as eskers deposited beneath a former Hesperian ice sheet or as resistant, inverted channel fills; with about 164 m of relief at 2 m post spacing, this DTM provides the cross-sectional profiles needed to tell those origins apart.
cite: Head, J. W., & Pratt, S. (2001). Extensive Hesperian-aged south polar ice sheet on Mars: Evidence for massive melting and retreat, and lateral flow and ponding of meltwater. Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets, 106(E6), 12275–12299. https://doi.org/10.1029/2000JE001359
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: Landing SpaceX Starship Phlegra
geo: This DTM covers terrain in the Phlegra region of the northern mid-latitudes that has been studied as a candidate landing area for SpaceX Starship. Radar, thermal, and geomorphic mapping by the Subsurface Water Ice Mapping (SWIM) project shows that water ice is likely within the upper few meters across much of this belt: a resource for future crewed missions and a constraint on landing-site engineering. Its mean offset from MOLA (-0.017 m) is the smallest in the portfolio.
cite: Morgan, G. A., Putzig, N. E., Perry, M. R., Sizemore, H. G., Bramson, A. M., Petersen, E. I., Bain, Z. M., Baker, D. M. H., Mastrogiuseppe, M., Hoover, R. H., Smith, I. B., Pathare, A., Dundas, C. M., & Campbell, B. A. (2021). Availability of subsurface water-ice resources in the northern mid-latitudes of Mars. Nature Astronomy, 5(3), 230–236. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41550-020-01290-z
coord_source: PDS DTM label (centre of MINIMUM/MAXIMUM_LATITUDE and WESTERNMOST/EASTERNMOST_LONGITUDE)

name: Guilled Crater
geo: This southern mid-latitude crater contains well-developed gullies on steep interior slopes. Martian gullies commonly consist of alcoves, channels, and depositional aprons, and repeat HiRISE imaging has shown that present-day modification at many mid- and high-latitude sites is strongly associated with seasonal carbon-dioxide frost processes.
cite: Dundas, C. M., Diniega, S., Hansen, C. J., Byrne, S., & McEwen, A. S. (2012). Seasonal activity and morphological changes in martian gullies. Icarus, 220(1), 124–143. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.icarus.2012.04.005

name: USGS Dune
geo: This high-southern-latitude dune field provides topographic control on dune morphology in a terrain affected by strong seasonal carbon-dioxide frost cycles. Repeat HiRISE observations of polar and subpolar dunes show that frost-related mass movement can modify dune slopes and gullies on present-day Mars.
cite: Diniega, S., Byrne, S., Bridges, N. T., Dundas, C. M., & McEwen, A. S. (2010). Seasonality of present-day Martian dune-gully activity. Geology, 38(11), 1047–1050. https://doi.org/10.1130/g31287.1
